opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think people sometimes assume the two are more tangled up than they really are. The simplest way I'd put it is that we share a lot of the same instincts about where things are heading. We both believe reinforcement learning on open models is going to be a huge part of the story, and that the tooling for doing it well shouldn't live only inside a handful of big labs. So there's a lot of natural overlap, and that's where the collaboration comes from.

At Prime Intellect, a lot of my focus is very infrastructure- and ecosystem-shaped. How do you make it easy for anyone to define an environment, plug in a reward signal, and actually train against it at scale, across distributed compute that isn't one giant cluster? That's things like the verifiers work, the environments hub, making the whole loop of "write a task, evaluate a model, train on it" feel like a normal software engineering workflow instead of research heroics.

The way I think about RCI's priorities is that they're coming at it more from the research question side. What are the right problems to be asking? What does good evaluation look like? Where does RL actually generalize, and where is it just teaching the model to game a specific setup? Those are questions we care about too, but our job is to build the substrate that lets lots of people explore them, not necessarily to be the ones answering every one of them.

So the distinction is less about disagreement and more about division of labor. If we do our part well, groups like RCI can move faster because they're not rebuilding the plumbing every time. And if they do their part well, they surface failure modes and research directions that tell us what the infrastructure actually needs to support. That feedback loop is the valuable thing. Honestly, I'd love for there to be many more relationships like that, because the open ecosystem only works if the people building tools and the people asking hard research questions are actually talking to each other.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'd describe it as a pretty natural division of labor, honestly. Prime Intellect's whole thesis is about building the open infrastructure layer: decentralized training, the environments hub, verifiers, making it so that anyone can spin up an RL environment and actually train against it without needing to be inside one of the big labs. That's the north star there. The bet is that the ecosystem of environments and the tooling around them is going to matter at least as much as any single model.

RCI comes at it from a different angle. The priority there is much more on the research question itself: what are the right tasks, what does good reward design actually look like, how do you evaluate whether an agent is genuinely getting better versus just overfitting to a verifier. It's less "let's ship infrastructure for everyone" and more "let's be rigorous about what we're actually measuring."

So where it overlaps is pretty obvious once you lay it out like that. We build environments, they stress-test them. They'll come back and say "your reward function is exploitable in this specific way," or "this benchmark saturates way too fast to be useful," and that feedback loop is honestly the most valuable part. A lot of RL environment work looks great on paper and falls apart the second a model finds the shortcut, and having people whose whole job is to find that shortcut before the model does is huge.

The friction, if there is any, is mostly around pace. Prime Intellect wants to move fast and get things in people's hands. The research side wants to be careful. I think that tension is actually healthy though. If it were all one culture you'd either ship a bunch of broken environments or you'd never ship anything. Having both pulling in slightly different directions ends up with something better than either would produce alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as very complementary. There’s a lot of overlap in what we want to make possible, but we’re approaching it from different directions. Prime Intellect is focused on the infrastructure side—making compute accessible and enabling people to train models together. At RCI, our emphasis is more on the research: what should we train, in which environments, and how do we get a meaningful improvement in capabilities?

Those things inform each other. The research pushes on what the infrastructure needs to support, and better infrastructure expands the experiments we can run. So collaborating makes sense without our priorities having to be identical.
